c1.story:
In September 2016 Mukesh Ambani walked on stage and announced that Reliance Jio would give India free voice calls and free data for months. Overnight, an industry that had argued over paise per minute found itself competing with zero. Within three years, most of the operators that had crowded the market were gone, merged or bankrupt, and the survivors were bleeding. Telecom in India is the story of what happened next, and to follow it you need to know that the word telecom covers four quite different businesses.

The first door is the operators, the companies whose name is on your SIM card: Bharti Airtel, its listed subsidiary Bharti Hexacom, which runs the network in Rajasthan and the Northeast, Vodafone Idea, and Tata Teleservices Maharashtra. Their revenue is simply subscribers times what each pays a month, and their fortunes turn on one thing: whether tariffs go up.

The second door is the landlords. Indus Towers owns a vast grid of steel towers and rents space on each to operators; Altius, a trust that holds the towers that once belonged to Jio, does the same. RailTel lays fibre along railway tracks. They charge rent per tenant per tower, pass the power bill through, and throw off cash. Their worry is not price but tenants: will all of them still be around to pay?

The third door is enterprise networks. Tata Communications, the old state-owned VSNL privatised in 2002, sells undersea cable capacity, cloud links and managed services to companies on long contracts. Its customer is corporate India and the world, not your phone bill.

The fourth door makes the hardware: HFCL and Vindhya with fibre and cable, Tejas Networks with routers and radios, Optiemus, Avantel, Valiant and Nelco with devices and satellite kit. They live on lumpy orders and starve between build cycles.

A tariff hike, a court ruling, a 5G auction: one headline, four very different reactions.
c1.read:
Four tiles, four doors. Read each top to bottom, then compare the profit bars.

  • The name and the line under it say how the money comes in: monthly plans, rent per tenant per tower, multi-year enterprise contracts, or one-off equipment orders.
  • The tickers are listed names behind each door; click to open a stock page. Notice RailTel appears twice, as a fibre landlord and an enterprise network, because it does both.
  • The profit bar is how much of each rupee the business keeps. Towers sit at high: once a tower stands, each extra tenant is almost pure profit, and contracts run for years. Operators sit at medium, not high, because the government and the equipment vendors take a big bite first. Enterprise networks sit at medium. Equipment makers sit at low, squeezed between a handful of huge buyers and foreign rivals.
  • The last line is the bet. Read the operator tile's closely: a market with only two and a half players. The half is Vodafone Idea, and it shapes every other tile.

Under the tiles, the housing society analogy maps the doors: operators collect maintenance from every flat, towers own the land and collect ground rent, enterprise wires up office parks, and equipment makers sell the cables and starve between projects.

The so-what line is your filter for news. An operator moves on tariffs, a tower stock on its tenants' health, an equipment stock on order flow. Before reacting to any telecom headline, ask which tile it actually touches.

c2.story:
Think of Indian telecom as a kitchen where the two most expensive ingredients are bought from people you cannot bargain with.

The first station is the government. Airwaves, the spectrum that carries your calls and data, are a national resource, and the Department of Telecommunications auctions them. Operators pay enormous sums, often in instalments that behave exactly like debt, and on top of that hand over a slice of their revenue every year as licence fees. When Vodafone Idea could not pay the dues piled up after the Supreme Court's 2019 ruling, the government converted them into shares. The state is now not just the operator's landlord but its largest shareholder.

The second station is equipment. Every tower needs radios, every network a core, every street fibre. India excludes Chinese vendors on security grounds, so operators buy radios from Ericsson, Nokia and Samsung, priced in dollars. Indian makers like Tejas, HFCL and Vindhya supply fibre and some network gear, and Tejas, working with the state-run C-DoT and TCS, built the radio network for BSNL's homegrown 4G.

The third station is the physical grid: steel towers, rooftop sites, diesel generators and the fibre that links them. Indus Towers, Altius, RailTel and Jio's own tower arm own most of it. The fourth is running the network: billing, customer care, the recharge counter at every kirana shop. That is Airtel, Jio, Vodafone Idea and the smaller listed names. The fifth station is you, and more than a billion people like you.

Here is the trap in this layout. Costs rise at the first two stations, when an auction is held or the rupee weakens, and the only place to recover them is the last station, by raising your tariff. That is why tariff hikes tend to follow auctions. The biggest player, Jio, has sat outside the stock market for its whole life; its 2026 IPO brings the largest operator into the listed universe at last.

The two costliest ingredients are bought from the state and from abroad. The only place to pass them on is your monthly bill.
c2.read:
Read the five boxes left to right, from the airwaves to the subscriber.

  • Spectrum and licences: the government auctions airwaves and takes a yearly fee on revenue.
  • Equipment: radios, core network, fibre and routers, mostly from Nordic and Korean vendors, with Indian makers in fibre and some gear.
  • Towers and fibre: the steel, the power and the cables at each site.
  • Network operations: running the network and selling plans.
  • Customer: prepaid, postpaid, home fibre and enterprise.

Now the band row. The first cell is government, the second carries the rival colour for the Nordic vendors, the third and fourth are coloured India listed, and the fifth is subscribers. The Indian listed value sits in the middle two stations, towers and network, and is fenced in on the left by two suppliers with strong pricing power: the state and foreign vendors.

The rival line adds a twist: besides the vendors, it names Starlink and satellite broadband as the coming substitute. That substitute does not sit on any station in this kitchen. It goes around the kitchen, from satellite straight to the subscriber, skipping towers and fibre entirely.

The note under the diagram says the costly stations are the first two. Use the layout as a cause-and-effect chain: news at the left end, an auction, a rupee slide, a vendor price rise, is a cost that must eventually be recovered at the right end. When you see one, start watching for the tariff hike. The so-what line makes exactly that link.

c3.story:
The money in Indian telecom arrives a few hundred rupees at a time, mostly through a recharge at a corner shop or a tap on a payments app. Prepaid mobile users are the bulk of the market, and they are the people every tariff hike is really tested on.

Here is how the test plays out. When the leaders raise prices, most users grumble and pay, because data has become as essential as electricity. But some drop their second SIM: millions of Indians carry two, one for cheap calls and one for data, and a hike is the moment to consolidate. Others move down to a cheaper plan. Watching subscriber numbers and plan mix in the two quarters after a hike tells you whether pricing power is real or borrowed.

Above the prepaid mass sits the premium tier: postpaid family plans, bundles with streaming apps, international roaming. These users move with urban incomes and are where operators push hardest to raise revenue per user. Home broadband is the quiet growth story, as fibre reaches apartment blocks and cable television fades; it moves with housing construction and the habits that work from home left behind.

Prepaid is where the money is. It is also where the political cost of every tariff hike gets paid.

Enterprises buy leased lines, cloud links and secure networks, and move with corporate technology budgets and the data-centre boom; that is Tata Communications' and RailTel's world. Government networks buy BSNL's equipment, railway and defence fibre and rural broadband, in budget cycles. Other operators are customers too, buying tower space, fibre leases and roaming, which is why a tower company's fate is tied to its tenants' solvency.

And then the machines: SIM cards inside cars, smart electricity meters and card terminals. Small today, but every smart-meter rollout is a few million connections that never complain about a tariff hike.
c3.read:
Seven tiles, seven customer groups. Each has three lines: who buys, what they buy, and what moves them.

Read the first tile first, as the so-what line under the grid tells you to. Prepaid mobile users buy monthly recharges, and what moves them is tariff hikes, rural incomes and smartphone prices. That third line is the most important watch list in the sector: after each hike, check whether users downgrade plans or drop a SIM.

Then group the remaining tiles:

  • Upgrade tiles: postpaid and premium users, and home broadband. These are where revenue per user grows beyond hikes, through better plans and bundles.
  • Business tiles: enterprises and government networks. These feed the enterprise door and the equipment makers, and they move with corporate IT budgets and budget allocations, not with consumer moods.
  • Industry tiles: other operators, and machines and devices. The first is how the tower landlords earn; its third line, rival capex and solvency, is the tower investor's whole worry. The second is a small, steady add-on.

Now link the tiles to card one's doors. Operators live on the first three tiles. Towers live almost entirely on the other-operators tile, which is why three tenants, one of them fragile, matter so much. Tata Communications and RailTel live on enterprises and government. Equipment makers depend on government networks and operator capex. If a company you own draws most of its revenue from a single tile, its third line is your single most important indicator.

c4.story:
The explainer calls a telecom operator a toll road built with borrowed money, and it is worth taking the analogy seriously, because it explains almost every line of the accounts.

Building the road is brutally expensive. Spectrum is bought at auction for sums that run into the tens of thousands of crores, often paid in instalments that are debt in all but name. Then every tower needs radios, every site needs power and every city needs fibre. All of that gets written off over many years as depreciation and amortisation, and the borrowed money behind it carries interest. Together, those two lines can swallow a huge share of revenue, which is why a telecom company can have a magnificent operating margin and a thin, or negative, net profit in the same year.

Running the road is cheap by comparison. Once the network exists, carrying one more subscriber, or one more gigabyte, costs almost nothing. So every tariff hike flows almost straight to profit. Before anything else, though, the government takes its cut: licence fees and spectrum charges are a fixed slice of revenue.

A telecom operator's EBITDA belongs to the shareholders only after the government, the lenders and the next network upgrade have been paid.

The tower company is a different animal on the same road. Its biggest cost line is power and fuel at the sites, but most of that is passed through to tenants, so it is closer to a reimbursement than a cost. Depreciation and interest are large too, because towers are steel and steel is capital. But each additional tenant on an existing tower costs very little, so tenancy is to a tower what tariffs are to an operator.

Working capital tells the last part of the story. Prepaid users pay in advance, a gift to operators. Tower companies are owed money by their tenants, and when one tenant is in financial trouble, those receivables are where it shows first.
c4.read:
Two bar charts walk one hundred rupees of revenue down to what is left: integrated operators on the left, tower and fibre landlords on the right. Read each left to right.

  • The first bar is the full hundred rupees.
  • Network cost, the input bar, includes tower rent, power, licence and spectrum fees. It takes a bit under four of every ten rupees in both charts, but it means different things: for operators it is largely rent and government fees, for towers largely power passed through to tenants.
  • People, sales, marketing and customer care is modest in both, a little over a tenth for operators and a tenth for towers. Telecom is not a people business.
  • Depreciation and interest is the bar to stare at. For operators it takes roughly three of every ten rupees, for towers a quarter. Compare that with an IT services chart, where this bar is a sliver. This is what a capital-heavy, debt-funded business looks like.
  • What is left is about a fifth for operators and a little under three in ten for towers. The landlord keeps more than the tenant.

These are illustrative mid-cycle shapes; hover a bar for amounts.

Below the charts, the list marks what matters, and it is unusually long: revenue per user, depreciation and amortisation, interest and deferred spectrum dues, capex, and licence fees all get a yes. Working capital and energy get a sometimes. Tax gets a no, because years of losses left large tax credits. The so-what line gives the one pairing to watch: revenue per user rising while capex falls below depreciation. That is the free-cash-flow phase.

c5.story:
Most industries cycle with the economy. Indian telecom cycles with competition, and its cycles are long, painful and very readable.

The last full lap started with a crowded boom. In the early 2010s data was taking off and something like a dozen operators chased subscribers across the country. Then came the turn. In 2016 the government held a record spectrum auction, and that September Jio launched with months of free service. Tariffs collapsed. Telenor sold its Indian business to Airtel, Aircel went bankrupt, Tata's consumer mobile business was handed to Airtel, and Vodafone and Idea merged in 2018 to survive. In October 2019 the Supreme Court ruled that adjusted gross revenue, the base for licence fees, included non-telecom income, landing enormous back dues on the operators. The industry earned nothing for years.

The bottom was reached when there was nobody left to fight. With three private players, the operators raised tariffs together in December 2019, then again in late 2021, after a government relief package offered a moratorium on dues and the option to convert interest into equity. The first 5G auction in 2022 forced a final burst of record capex, which Jio and Airtel could afford and Vodafone Idea could not.

Then the harvest began. A third round of hikes in mid 2024, roughly a fifth higher, went through. By 2025 the 5G build had matured, capex fell, and free cash flow jumped. Starlink won its licence, the government moved to ease Vodafone Idea's dues, and trusted-source rules handed BSNL's 4G build to Tejas and C-DoT.

The price war ended the way price wars usually do: when there were not enough players left to fight it.

Now, in 2026, Jio's long-awaited listing is set to give the whole sector a public benchmark, and the market waits to see whether the next tariff hike follows it.
c5.read:
Three pieces: the clock, the timeline and the four hands. One quirk to grasp first: the arc years and the arrow describe two different laps.

The clock has four arcs clockwise from the top. The years under them are the previous lap: the boom of 2012 to 2015, the peak of 2016, the bust from 2016 to 2019, and the bottom of 2019 and 2020. The arrow, though, points into the boom arc, labelled mid up-cycle. The industry has gone round once and is now climbing a new lap that began with the first hike in 2019. Hover an arc to read what defined it last time.

The timeline runs from 2019 and shows the new lap: 2019 coloured bust, the court ruling year; 2020 to 2022 neutral, the repair years; 2023 to 2025 coloured boom, as hikes and falling capex turned into cash; and 2026 marked now.

The four hands:

  • Average revenue per user: rising steadily, an up arrow. Rising without subscriber loss is pricing power intact.
  • Capex to depreciation: falling below one, also an up arrow, because falling capex is good news here. A jump would mean a new build cycle.
  • Vodafone Idea's cash position: fragile and state-supported, mixed. Its survival keeps three players and a third tower tenant.
  • Satellite broadband pricing: launching at premium prices, flat for now.

Two hands up, one mixed, one flat: a healthy middle of the up-cycle. The so-what line says who gains: the operator with the best balance sheet first, towers second, equipment makers not until the next build wave.

c6.story:
For a telecom company, two numbers decide almost everything: what customers pay and what lenders charge.

The first is tariffs. A hike flows into revenue per user within two quarters as prepaid users recharge at the new price, and because the network is already built, almost all of it drops to operating profit. No other dial comes close in force. The second is interest rates. Operators and tower trusts carry heavy debt, including spectrum dues owed to the government, so every move in rates changes how much of that operating profit survives to the bottom line. A highly leveraged operator can see a hike's benefit eaten by a rate rise.

Tariffs decide the revenue line. Interest rates decide whether anything is left after the spectrum bill.

Then come the middleweights. The rupee matters because radios are bought from abroad in dollars and some debt is in dollars too; a weaker rupee makes both dearer. Spectrum auctions are two-faced: they add debt and amortisation, but history shows they also trigger the next tariff hike. Rural incomes and inflation decide how much of a hike prepaid users can absorb before they drop a SIM. Smartphone sales pull users onto costlier data plans. And the twin dial of the China gear ban and satellite entry cuts both ways: the ban protects Indian gear makers but keeps operator costs high, while satellite broadband threatens rural pricing.

The light dials matter mostly to the landlords and to valuation. Diesel and power prices raise tower costs, though most is passed through. Global equity liquidity decides how hungrily big listings like Jio's are received and how richly dividend stocks are priced. And US bond yields are the yardstick global investors hold up against tower-trust yields: when Treasuries pay more, an Indian tower trust's dividend looks thinner.
c6.read:
Each row is a dial: the outside force, its channel into profits, what a rise does, its weight, and today's reading where it maps to a series we track.

  • The arrow: green up means a rise helps, red down means it hurts, a diamond means it cuts both ways.
  • The dots: one to three for how much the dial matters.

Scan the three-dot rows first: tariff hikes and interest rates. Exactly as the so-what line says, these two run the sector. Tariffs carry no live series; you learn about them from operator announcements. Interest rates map to the Indian money rate, so the last column shows its latest value.

Now count the colours, because this table looks very different from an IT or software table. Five dials are red: interest rates, the rupee, rural inflation, diesel and power, and US bond yields. Only three are green: tariffs, smartphone sales and global liquidity. That colour balance is the signature of a capital-heavy, import-dependent, debt-funded industry. Most outside forces hurt it; the main thing that helps is its own pricing.

The two diamonds, spectrum auctions and the China gear ban with satellite entry, are the policy dials, and both cut differently for different doors: an auction hurts operators now but helps them later through hikes; the gear ban helps Indian equipment makers and hurts operators.

Seven rows map to series: the money rate, the rupee, consumer inflation, crude for diesel, consumer-durables output for smartphones, the Nifty for liquidity, and the US ten-year yield. The rest show a dash.

c7.story:
For most of the last decade, Indian telecom was a business that served more than a billion people and made almost no money. The bottlenecks on this card explain why, and how much of the current recovery the operators get to keep.

The first is that the government takes its cut before anyone else. Licence fees and spectrum charges come off the top of revenue, and auction prices in India have been among the steepest in the world relative to what users pay. The second is the shape of the market: two and a half players. Jio and Airtel set prices; Vodafone Idea follows; the state-owned BSNL lags. A hike needs the two leaders to move together, and the regulator has so far let them. That is a gift in an up-cycle and a reminder in a down one that pricing is a shared decision.

Then come the forces that cap the upside. Vodafone Idea's survival is a recurring drama: if it collapsed, its subscribers would pour onto two networks, the tower companies would lose a big tenant, and the government, as its largest shareholder, would book the loss. So the state keeps it alive, which preserves a third competitor. And Indians are used to some of the cheapest data on earth. Tariff hikes carry a political cost, so pricing power gets used in steps every few years, not continuously.

The leaders can raise prices. They just cannot raise them often, or alone.

The structural supply bottleneck is imported radios: with Chinese vendors banned, operators depend on Ericsson, Nokia and Samsung, priced in dollars. Right-of-way permissions for every tower and trench still flare up state by state. Each network generation forces a multi-year spend before revenue follows, and 5G has yet to find something users will happily pay extra for. And on the horizon sits satellite broadband, expensive today, but a potential ceiling on rural prices tomorrow.
c7.read:
Each row is a bottleneck, its reason and a severity label. In this card the label matters as much as the row.

  • Structural: the government's first cut, low prices by habit, and imported radios. Three permanent rows. They cap returns through every cycle and belong in your long-run valuation.
  • Two-sided: two and a half players. It allows coordinated hikes, the engine of the current up-cycle, but it also means a regulator's change of mood or one leader breaking ranks could end the party.
  • Recurring: Vodafone Idea's survival, and right-of-way disputes. These produce the headlines. Vodafone Idea's funding news moves three sets of stocks at once: its own, the leaders' and the towers'.
  • Cyclical: lumpy capex generations. Quiet now that 5G is built; loud again when the next generation arrives.
  • Slow: satellite substitution, which is far off but has a long reach.

The so-what line tells you how to read the ordering. The first two rows explain the lost decade: a big government cut and, until consolidation, too many players. The third and fourth rows, Vodafone Idea's survival and the habit of low prices, decide how much of the current up-cycle the leaders keep. When you weigh an operator stock today, it is those two rows, not the structural ones, that will decide the next few years.

c8.story:
No Indian industry has been shaped more by its rulebook than telecom. Courts, ministries and the regulator have, at different moments, created the industry's boom, nearly destroyed it, and then nursed it back to health.

Start with the courts. In 2012 the Supreme Court cancelled a large batch of mobile licences after the spectrum allocation scandal of the late 2000s, forcing spectrum to be sold by auction from then on, at prices that later weighed on every balance sheet. In October 2019 it went further, defining adjusted gross revenue, the base for licence fees, to include non-telecom income. That single definition created back dues so large that Vodafone Idea could only survive by turning the government into its largest shareholder. Relief headlines on those dues still move the stock more than its quarterly results.

The Department of Telecommunications is the industry's biggest single cost line: it issues licences, runs auctions, collects fees and, through the trusted-source rules, decides which vendors may supply the network. Chinese gear is effectively excluded, which protects Indian makers and BSNL's homegrown network but raises operator costs. The production-linked incentive for telecom equipment adds subsidies for local manufacturing.

In Indian telecom, a court definition once did more damage than a decade of price war.

TRAI, the regulator, matters as much for what it does not do. Under tariff forbearance, it lets operators set prices freely, which is what made the coordinated hikes since 2019 possible. Any change of mood there would matter enormously.

The newest rules point to the future. The Telecommunications Act of 2023 replaced a law from the telegraph era and allows satellite spectrum to be assigned administratively rather than auctioned, which opened the door to Starlink and was fiercely opposed by the operators. The Right of Way Rules of 2024 standardise fees and timelines for towers and fibre. And the pricing of satellite spectrum, still being set, will decide how cheap satellite broadband can be.
c8.read:
Each row is a regulator or rule: what it does, why you care, and a status tag. Read the status column to prioritise.

  • Always: the Department of Telecommunications, TRAI and the appeals tribunal, TDSAT. These are the permanent institutions. Two lines deserve a highlight: DoT is the biggest cost line, and TRAI's hands-off stance on tariffs is the quiet foundation of the up-cycle.
  • Live: the Telecommunications Act of 2023, the Supreme Court AGR judgment and its later relief, trusted-source rules, and the equipment incentive scheme. These are actively shaping cash flows now. The AGR row is the one that moves Vodafone Idea; the trusted-source and incentive rows are the ones that move equipment makers.
  • New: the Right of Way Rules of 2024, a slow positive for towers and fibre.
  • Coming: satellite spectrum pricing. A single row, but it decides how hard the substitute in card two can hit rural and broadband pricing.

A useful exercise is to map rows to doors. Operators care most about DoT, TRAI and AGR. Towers care about right of way and their tenants' AGR relief. Equipment makers care about trusted sources and the incentive scheme. Satellite pricing touches everyone, slowly.

Dated regulatory news for this industry, filtered from our feed, sits on the Picks and signals tab. In telecom it is worth reading weekly, because rule changes here move stocks the day they land.

c9.story:
Run Indian telecom through Porter's five forces and you get a surprise: the operators and the tower companies, which share the same towers and the same customers, have almost opposite profiles.

Start with the operators. Rivalry is moderate, because two leaders price together and a weakened third follows. New entrants are almost impossible: buying spectrum, building a national network and surviving the years of losses it takes to fill one requires the balance sheet of Reliance, and even Reliance needed years and a free-service war to get there. Buyers have almost no power: a billion prepaid users cannot negotiate, they can only grumble or drop a second SIM. So far, so wonderful. The problem is suppliers. The government sells spectrum at auction prices it sets and takes a fee on revenue; the equipment vendors are a small club of foreign giants. That one spoke is where operator profits leak.

Now the towers. Each tower is a little local monopoly: an operator wanting coverage on that hill rents space there, so rivalry is low. Suppliers, steel, land and power, are manageable. But look at the buyers: a tower company has three tenants, and one of them is fragile. When Vodafone Idea delays payments, a tower company's receivables swell and dividends wobble. That single spoke dominates the tower investment case.

The operator's problem is the people it buys from. The tower's problem is the people it sells to.

Substitutes are a slow threat to both. Wi-Fi offloads data from mobile networks, satellites can reach where towers cannot, and an operator can always build its own towers instead of renting them. None of these bites hard today, but each puts a ceiling on how far either door can push.
c9.read:
The radar has five spokes, one per force. The further a shape reaches along a spoke, the more pressure, so a smaller shape is the better business.

Two shapes are drawn, and they look like two kites pointing in different directions. The integrated operators' shape spikes out to the outer ring on supplier power and stays tight everywhere else, tightest of all on entrants. The towers and fibre landlords' shape spikes out to the outer ring on buyer power and is moderate elsewhere.

Read the spikes, because each one is the whole story for its door:

  • Operators, supplier spoke: the government's spectrum and the foreign vendors' radios. Watch auctions and the rupee.
  • Towers, buyer spoke: three tenants, one fragile. Watch Vodafone Idea's funding.

Then compare spoke by spoke. Operators feel more pressure on rivalry and suppliers. Towers feel more on buyers, entrants and substitutes, because an operator can always build its own towers instead of renting. The entrants spoke is low for both: nobody is starting a new national network, and even a tower grid is slow and costly to copy.

The table beside the chart gives each score from zero to three with its reason. Check the buyer row's reason for towers; it is the single sentence a tower investor needs to remember.

The so-what line ranks the doors: operators keep the profit when only two are strong, towers keep a steady share as long as tenants pay, and equipment makers, not drawn on the radar, keep the least. If Vodafone Idea's finances were ever fully repaired, the tower shape's buyer spike would shrink, and that is the single biggest re-rating lever for the landlords.

c10.story:
Telecom results come with a fat investor deck: subscriber bases by circle, data usage per user, minutes of use, tower counts, 5G sites. Eight numbers cut through it.

The first is average revenue per user, the sector's heartbeat. It moves with tariff hikes, with users upgrading from feature phones to smartphones and from prepaid to postpaid, and with plan mix. Airtel's management has long argued the industry needs far higher revenue per user to earn a fair return on its spectrum and network; the good column puts a figure on that target. The second is subscriber and 4G and 5G adds, which tells you whether a hike cost customers and whether users are trading up.

Then operating leverage. EBITDA margin shows how much of each rupee of revenue survives network and staff costs. In telecom it can look spectacular, which is why the next numbers matter more. Capex to depreciation says whether the company is building or harvesting: below one is harvest, above one and a half is a new rollout wave.

A telecom EBITDA margin is a promise. Capex, interest and dividends tell you whether it is kept.

Then the balance sheet, because this is a debt-funded business. Net debt to EBITDA tells you whether the company can carry the next auction. Interest as a share of EBITDA tells you how much of the operating profit goes to lenders and the government before shareholders see anything. Vodafone Idea is the cautionary example on both.

For the landlords, the tenancy ratio, how many operators share each tower, is the growth engine, and tenant receivables are the stress gauge. Finally, the number that justifies the whole cycle: free cash flow and the dividend. An up-cycle only matters to shareholders if it reaches them, and in the harvest phase this is where it should show.
c10.read:
Eight rows: the number, what it tells you, what good looks like, and today's industry median from listed companies' latest filings.

  • What it tells you is the question to ask of every company.
  • What good looks like carries the figures. Several rows give separate marks for operators and towers, so apply the right one. The revenue-per-user row also gives the industry's stated target, a useful yardstick for how far the hikes still have to run.
  • Today's median is the typical listed company. The first two rows, revenue per user and subscriber adds, show a dash: operators report them in their decks, not in the filing lines we hold.

Read two of the medians with care, because they are proxies. The tenancy row's median is receivable days, which speaks to the tenant-receivables half of that row but not to tenancy itself. The free-cash-flow row's median is return on capital, the nearest filing line, which tells you whether the capital earns its keep but is not the same as cash reaching shareholders.

Remember too that the median mixes all four doors: operators, towers, Tata Communications, and equipment makers big and small. It will rarely look like any one operator. The useful comparison for each company is three-way: its own number, the median and the good mark for its door. For an operator, start with capex to depreciation and interest share of EBITDA; for a tower company, start with receivable days. Those are the rows where this cycle is won or lost.

c11.story:
Telecom gives you some of the longest early warnings of any sector, because so much of it runs on announced decisions that take time to show up in the numbers.

The furthest-reaching signal is satellite broadband pricing. When Starlink and its rivals publish their plans, they set a ceiling on what rural and home-broadband users will pay, long before any subscriber actually switches. That speaks three quarters or more ahead.

Two quarters ahead sit three signals. A leader's tariff announcement is the strongest: prepaid users recharge over the following months, so revenue per user climbs with a lag, and you can model the next two quarters the day the press release lands. Smartphone shipments, especially 5G handsets, tell you who will upgrade plans. And BSNL and government network tenders become revenue for Indian gear makers about two quarters after they are awarded.

A quarter ahead, the money signals: the spectrum auction calendar and reserve prices, which add debt first and usually trigger a hike next; the repo rate and bond yields, which set refinancing costs and the yardstick for tower-trust yields; and the rupee, which reprices equipment contracts. In the same quarter, the headline that moves everything: Vodafone Idea's funding and government relief.

Put the core signals together and you get the rule. The industry is in an up-cycle when revenue per user is rising without subscriber loss, capex is below depreciation, and the weakest operator is funded enough to stay in the market. Today all three are ticking. Revenue per user is climbing at the leaders, the 5G build is maturing, and state relief keeps Vodafone Idea alive, if fragile.

Three ticks out of three, with the third written in pencil.

Hence the call: a mid up-cycle with cash arriving. Prefer the best-balance-sheet operator and the tower landlords over the stressed third player and the equipment makers, who need a new build wave this phase does not give them.

The lead-time chart places each outside signal by how far ahead it speaks; the further right a dot, the earlier the warning. Telecom is the rare industry with a dot in every column.

  • Same quarter: Vodafone Idea funding and relief headlines. These move tower occupancy and the market structure at once.
  • One quarter ahead: the spectrum auction calendar, the repo rate and bond yields, and the rupee. The money cluster.
  • Two quarters ahead: a leader's tariff announcement, smartphone shipments, and BSNL and government tenders. The revenue cluster.
  • Three or more: satellite plan pricing, alone on the far right, the slowest-burning threat.

Hover a dot to read its channel. A good reading order is right to left: check the satellite dot for long-run pricing, the two-quarter cluster for revenue direction, the one-quarter cluster for cost of money, and the same-quarter dot for the market-structure risk.

Below the chart, the rule shows its three signs, all ticked: revenue per user rising with stable subscribers, capex below depreciation, and the weakest operator funded. Read the notes, though. The third tick is annotated still fragile. By the rule's wording, losing one tick still leaves the cycle intact; losing two means it is ending.

The call box gives the view, three supporting points and what would change it. The would-change list maps neatly onto the signs: visible SIM drops after a hike would break the first, a high-priced auction would hit the second, and cheap satellite plans or a state-funded fourth operator through BSNL would challenge the market structure the whole call rests on.
